meta.title: Who really said "It's tough to make predictions, especially about the future"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Yogi Berra. Quote Investigator traces it to an anonymous Danish saying, first in print in K. K. Steincke's 1948 memoir. Wikiquote files it as misattributed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's tough to make predictions, especially about the future'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Yogi Berra. It's an anonymous Danish proverb, earliest known in print in 1948 — decades before Berra's name was ever attached to it.

answer.label: Not Yogi Berra — an anonymous Danish saying
answer.authorDates: Earliest known in print 1948 · recorded by Danish politician K. K. Steincke
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator concludes that this comical proverb was first expressed in Danish and that its author remains unknown ↗, with the first written instance now known dated 1948, in the memoir Farvel og Tak by K. K. Steincke. English Wikiquote files the Berra version under its Misattributed section ↗; the earliest linkage of Berra’s name to the saying that QI documents is a 1991 newspaper article, and the wording quoted there was “I never make predictions, especially about the future.”

source.heading: The earliest documented instance

docMeta.dd: Farvel og Tak: Minder og Meninger — Ogsaa en Tilværelse IV (1935–1939)
Danish; the familiar English wording is an anonymous later rendering

source.excerpt:
Det er vanskeligt at spaa, især naar det gælder Fremtiden.
“It is difficult to make predictions, especially about the future.”
trail: 1948 — the first written instance now known appears in K. K. Steincke’s memoir Farvel og Tak, in Danish, presented as a remark from the parliamentary year 1937–1938 with no attribution, per Quote Investigator ↗.

1956 — the earliest English appearance QI records is in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, where the writer explicitly calls it a Danish proverb rather than anyone’s coinage — also discussed on the American Dialect Society list ↗.
1971 — Niels Bohr is credited for the first time, in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, nine years after his death, according to Quote Investigator ↗.

1991 — the earliest Berra linkage QI documents: a Richmond Times-Dispatch piece quoting “In the words of Yogi Berra, ‘I never make predictions, especially about the future’” — see Quote Investigator ↗ and the Wikiquote Misattributed list ↗.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator reports that Steincke presented the remark as having been spoken during the parliamentary year 1937–1938, with no attribution specified. The Danish sentence and QI’s English rendering are quoted here as QI gives them.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the popular English wording: it is an anonymous rendering of a Danish saying whose author is unknown, so there is no identifiable work or first-publication date behind this exact sentence. The one documented source, Steincke’s Farvel og Tak, was published in 1948 — well after 1930, the current US public-domain cutoff for published works — so nothing here should be treated as public domain.

author.name: K. K. Steincke
author.heading: Who actually wrote it down
author.metaLine: Karl Kristian Steincke, 1880–1963 · Danish Social Democratic politician, Minister of Justice and Minister of Social Affairs
author.bio: Steincke was a Danish Social Democrat who served as Minister of Justice and Minister of Social Affairs and is remembered as a principal architect of Denmark’s early welfare state. Late in his career he wrote a multi-volume memoir, Ogsaa en Tilværelse; the fourth volume, Farvel og Tak (1948), contains the earliest instance of this joke that Quote Investigator has located. Steincke is the recorder, not the proven author — he presented the line as something said in parliament, with no attribution given.

misattribution.heading: Everyone gets credit except the person who said it
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-adopted orphan jokes in English. Four famous names have been handed it, and Quote Investigator finds documentary support for none of them as originator.

items.why: English Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section ↗, noting the earliest citations describe the proverb as Danish. The earliest Berra linkage Quote Investigator documents is a 1991 Richmond Times-Dispatch article ↗, and even there the wording is “I never make predictions, especially about the future.”

Bohr was first credited in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists in 1971, nine years after his death, and Stanislaw Ulam credited him in 1976; Quote Investigator finds substantive evidence that Bohr used the saying in 1962 or earlier, though the exact date remains uncertain — but nothing showing he coined it ↗. QI also records the saying being credited in Danish sources of the early 1950s to the artist Robert Storm Petersen, a separate attribution it lists as pending verification.
The first Goldwyn attribution QI finds is in The Economist in 1979, after his death; QI calls the evidence for Goldwyn’s authorship very weak ↗.
A 1998 book by Keith J. Laidler suggested Twain used the formulation, but QI notes no corroborating evidence is presented ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody knows who coined it. Quote Investigator concludes the proverb was first expressed in Danish by an unknown author ↗, and the first written instance now known dates to 1948.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Yogi
lead: The joke works because it eats its own tail: a prediction is by definition about the future, so “especially about the future” is pure redundancy dressed as caution. That shape — a sentence that collapses on itself but still sounds wise — is exactly the shape of a Yogi-ism, which is why the line drifted onto Berra and stayed there.

But the paper trail runs through Copenhagen, not the Bronx. The first English appearance Quote Investigator records is a 1956 statistics journal where the writer explicitly flags it as a Danish proverb rather than anyone’s original quip — a tell that by then it was already folk property.
detailsBody: Niels Bohr is the other great magnet for this line, and he has a slightly better claim than Berra: Quote Investigator notes that Bohr was first credited in print in 1971, nine years after his death, that mathematician Stanislaw Ulam credited him in Adventures of a Mathematician (1976), and that there is substantive evidence he was using the saying by 1962 — though nothing showing he coined it. The Danish cartoonist Robert Storm Petersen is credited in early-1950s Danish sources QI lists as pending verification, and the claim that Bohr himself pointed at Storm P. comes from the American Dialect Society thread ↗, not from QI — and Storm P. does not appear to have originated it either.

Sam Goldwyn and Mark Twain have also been handed the line. QI dates the first Goldwyn attribution to 1979, five years after his death, and calls the evidence for his authorship very weak; the Twain version surfaces in a 1998 book with no corroborating citation. The pattern is the usual one: a jokey orphan proverb gets adopted by whichever famous wit the writer finds handiest.
context.pull: A prediction is already about the future. That’s the joke — and it was being told in Danish long before it was told in English.
